combos.name: Planned Public Economy
combos.summary: The state plans most of the economy, but ownership is shared with workers and public bodies instead of being fully centralized.

views.Healthcare: Universal, free and publicly run, with local and worker-run clinics alongside state hospitals.
views.Poverty & welfare: Guaranteed basics for everyone, with public and worker-owned enterprises providing housing and food.
views.Employment & labor: Jobs planned or guaranteed by the public sector, with workers given a real voice in management.
views.Taxes: Little personal taxation. Public enterprises fund services directly, with high taxes on any private wealth.
views.Business & markets: Core industries are planned and run with worker councils, and small private business is allowed at the edges.
views.Property & land: Land and industry are owned collectively, with use rights and shares held by workers and communities.
views.Education: Free and public through university, with workplaces and communities co-running training.
views.Environment & energy: Central planning of energy and resources, with local communities having a say in how projects are run.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a public planning office houses them and assigns them a job, with a residents' council helping them settle in.
You have a horrible cut, so a planned public hospital stitches you up free, and a staff and patient council runs the place.
You have an idea for a new business, so you pitch it to a planning council, which may fund it as a public-owned enterprise, with you as a worker-manager.
You lose your job, so a planned jobs board places you elsewhere in the public sector, so you don't lose income.
You want to buy or build a home, so you are given public housing, and ownership of a home is mostly collective.

combos.name: Mixed Public Economy
combos.summary: Key industries and utilities are public or worker owned, while the rest of the economy is private but actively regulated.

views.Healthcare: A public option or single-payer system funded by government, with private providers inside strict rules.
views.Poverty & welfare: A robust safety net plus public housing and jobs programs.
views.Employment & labor: Strong unions and worker boards, plus minimum wages and public jobs in downturns.
views.Taxes: High progressive taxes on income and wealth fund public ownership and programs.
views.Business & markets: Public ownership of utilities and finance, with strong regulation of the remaining private firms.
views.Property & land: A mix of public and private ownership: public control of essential assets and strict rules on private ones.
views.Education: Free public schooling and affordable or free college funded by government.
views.Environment & energy: Public investment and ownership of clean energy, backed by tough regulation.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a public housing office places them in a state-built unit, since the market doesn't build for people like them.
You have a horrible cut, so you go to a public hospital that treats you free or cheaply, while private ones are also open.
You have an idea for a new business, so you can start small on your own with loans from public programs, while big industries stay public.
You lose your job, so unemployment insurance pays part of your wage, and public employers are often hiring.
You want to buy or build a home, so you rent public housing or buy with a government-backed loan.

combos.name: Managed Capitalism
combos.summary: Large corporations drive the economy, but government steers them through regulation, subsidies and public investment.

views.Healthcare: Private insurers and providers backed by government programs and mandates.
views.Poverty & welfare: A safety net that supports workers and consumers so big business can keep growing, mostly linked to work.
views.Employment & labor: Big employers dominate, with government setting minimum standards and backing negotiation with unions.
views.Taxes: A progressive tax code with many breaks and credits tied to business investment.
views.Business & markets: Government and large firms cooperate on strategy, with rules to limit excesses and bailouts to prevent collapse.
views.Property & land: Strong corporate property rights, with government rules on use, antitrust and public interest.
views.Education: Public schools plus employer-linked training and government-funded university research.
views.Environment & energy: Regulation and subsidies guide large industries toward cleaner energy.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a government program gives a basic floor of help, but a private shelter or landlord provides the actual bed.
You have a horrible cut, so you are treated at a private hospital, and public insurance or your own plan pays, with a gap you may owe.
You have an idea for a new business, so you look for investors or a loan, with a few government programs helping small firms against large ones.
You lose your job, so unemployment insurance pays part of your wage while you search at large firms.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy from a large developer with a government-backed mortgage.

combos.name: Social Partnership
combos.summary: Unions, employer associations and the state bargain together over wages, benefits and economic policy.

views.Healthcare: Universal tax-funded care, with unions and associations helping plan and run it.
views.Poverty & welfare: Generous benefits, partly administered by union-linked funds.
views.Employment & labor: Industry-wide collective agreements set pay and conditions, with very high union membership.
views.Taxes: High broad-based taxes plus contributions to joint funds run by unions and employers.
views.Business & markets: Open markets, with firms organized in employer associations that bargain with unions.
views.Property & land: Private property, with a strong worker and trade association role in how firms are run.
views.Education: Free public schooling with apprenticeship and vocational training run jointly with the trades.
views.Environment & energy: Industry and union agreements work alongside government climate targets.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so their union and the state work together to place them in housing and a job.
You have a horrible cut, so the union health fund and the public clinic split the bill, so you pay very little.
You have an idea for a new business, so your guild and public programs back you, and you start within an organized trade with training provided.
You lose your job, so your union finds you work and public unemployment pay covers you meanwhile.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy or rent with help from your union and public loans.

combos.name: Coordinated Market Economy
combos.summary: Competitive private markets sit inside a network of strong social insurance, worker representation and long-term coordination.

views.Healthcare: Universal coverage through public or tightly regulated insurance.
views.Poverty & welfare: Broad social insurance plus a strong safety net for those left out.
views.Employment & labor: Collective bargaining, works councils and board seats for workers, with strong training.
views.Taxes: High taxes and contributions funding social insurance.
views.Business & markets: Competitive markets under strong rules, with long-term financing and cooperation between firms, banks and unions.
views.Property & land: Private property with social obligations, plus some public ownership of key utilities.
views.Education: Free or cheap schooling and university, with strong vocational and apprenticeship routes.
views.Environment & energy: Ambitious climate policy using carbon pricing and strong industry standards.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a caseworker arranges rent support quickly, and they find a room in a market for housing.
You have a horrible cut, so your required insurance pays at a regulated price, and you leave with stitches and a small bill.
You have an idea for a new business, so you start with bank loans and public support, inside fair-competition rules.
You lose your job, so generous unemployment pay and a caseworker support you while you look.
You want to buy or build a home, so you take a regulated mortgage with strong buyer protections.

combos.name: Regulated Social Market
combos.summary: A market economy with clear rules and social insurance, but a lighter touch and lower taxes than the European welfare model.

views.Healthcare: Insurance-based care with regulation to ensure broad coverage and some competition.
views.Poverty & welfare: Social insurance for workers plus a targeted safety net with work requirements.
views.Employment & labor: Flexible markets with minimum standards, works councils and a moderate union role.
views.Taxes: Moderate taxes and social contributions.
views.Business & markets: Competition enforced by antitrust and consumer rules, with a light touch on everything else.
views.Property & land: Strong private rights, with limited social obligations through zoning and environmental rules.
views.Education: Public schools with choice, plus apprenticeships and subsidized college.
views.Environment & energy: Market tools such as cap-and-trade and incentives, set within government standards.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a shelter with public funding takes them in, and rent aid helps them find a place on the private market.
You have a horrible cut, so your required insurance covers the visit, with a moderate copay at a private hospital.
You have an idea for a new business, so you meet moderate rules and get a bank loan, with fair-competition rules to help you.
You lose your job, so you get unemployment pay and a job-search program while you look.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy with a bank loan, with some zoning and some buyer protections.

combos.name: Cooperative Commons
combos.summary: Voluntary cooperation: co-ops and mutual aid societies running on shared resources, with no central state.

views.Healthcare: Community clinics and mutual aid funds, with voluntary cooperation instead of state mandates.
views.Poverty & welfare: Shared resources and land dividends, plus mutual aid networks.
views.Employment & labor: Worker co-ops and self-employment, with no bosses and no state-run labor system.
views.Taxes: Few or none, with voluntary contributions and charges for use of shared resources.
views.Business & markets: Co-ops, credit unions and fair exchange, with no corporate privileges.
views.Property & land: Use-based possession of land and tools, with natural resources held in common.
views.Education: Community-run, voluntary and free schools and skill-sharing.
views.Environment & energy: Local commons management, with polluters accountable to the community.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a housing co-op takes them in, and a shared land payment gives them a little to live on.
You have a horrible cut, so a member-run clinic stitches you up, paid for by dues and a shared resource payment.
You have an idea for a new business, so you start a co-op with a mutual bank loan, with little red tape and a shared resource payment to help.
You lose your job, so your co-op and mutual aid group help you, and a shared payment tops up your income.
You want to buy or build a home, so you build on community land through a housing co-op and pay a land rent.

combos.name: Liberal Commons
combos.summary: Free markets and civil liberties, with natural resources like land shared by everyone.

views.Healthcare: Mostly voluntary and private, with mutual aid and some shared funding from resource dividends.
views.Poverty & welfare: Growth plus a basic dividend from shared resources, instead of a large welfare state.
views.Employment & labor: Free contracts with strong worker freedom and no state-granted corporate privilege.
views.Taxes: Low, simple taxes, with land and resource charges as the main source.
views.Business & markets: Free trade and open competition, with anti-monopoly rules and no special privileges.
views.Property & land: Strong private property in goods, with land and natural resources taxed or shared.
views.Education: Parent- and community-led choice among private schools, with open access.
views.Environment & energy: Resource charges and clear property rights make polluters pay for what they use.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a small basic payment and cheap, easy-to-build housing let them find a room on their own.
You have a horrible cut, so you pick any clinic and pay with a basic voucher or insurance you chose.
You have an idea for a new business, so you start with few licenses and cheap capital, and a basic payment cushions you if it fails.
You lose your job, so a basic payment and a flexible job market keep you going until you find work.
You want to buy or build a home, so you build with few permits on land you rent from the community.

combos.name: Minimal-State Liberalism
combos.summary: A very small state limited to protecting rights and contracts, with nearly everything else left to private choice.

views.Healthcare: Private payment and charity, with government staying out apart from basic public health.
views.Poverty & welfare: Charity and growth, with at most very limited relief.
views.Employment & labor: Free contracts and few labor rules.
views.Taxes: Very low, flat or minimal taxes.
views.Business & markets: Free trade and competition with few regulations, and courts enforcing contracts.
views.Property & land: Strong, nearly absolute private property rights.
views.Education: Mostly private schools and vouchers, with minimal state involvement.
views.Environment & energy: Property rights and court cases handle pollution, with little regulation.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so the market and charities are all that is available, so a private charity gives them a bed.
You have a horrible cut, so a private clinic stitches you up at its listed price, and charity or your own insurance pays.
You have an idea for a new business, so you open with almost no rules and raise money privately, and you keep your profits.
You lose your job, so you live on savings while a lightly regulated market hires you quickly.
You want to buy or build a home, so you build or buy with almost no permits, and the market sets the price.

combos.name: State-Run Guilds
combos.summary: The state organizes each industry into official associations that run production under its direction.

views.Healthcare: A state-run national service administered through trade or industry funds.
views.Poverty & welfare: State-guaranteed basics delivered through workplace and trade organizations.
views.Employment & labor: Workers belong to state-recognized trade bodies that set pay and conditions under national plans.
views.Taxes: Dues and contributions to state-controlled bodies, plus direct state revenue.
views.Business & markets: Industries organized into official associations under a national plan.
views.Property & land: Collective ownership managed by trade bodies under state direction.
views.Education: State schooling plus compulsory trade training run by the industry bodies.
views.Environment & energy: National plans, with industry bodies responsible for resource use in their trade.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so the state sends them to an official trade association, which gives them a bed and work under its rules.
You have a horrible cut, so your state-run guild clinic treats you, because your trade ties you to its health plan.
You have an idea for a new business, so you apply to your state-run trade association, which may license you and sets the standards.
You lose your job, so the state places you in another guild shop with the same trade.
You want to buy or build a home, so your guild is given state housing blocks for members to live in.

combos.name: Cooperative Guilds
combos.summary: Trades and crafts organize themselves into member-owned guilds and co-ops that look after their own.

views.Healthcare: Guild and co-op benefit funds and community clinics.
views.Poverty & welfare: Mutual aid within the guild and community.
views.Employment & labor: Member-owned workshops and co-ops, with apprenticeships and shared standards.
views.Taxes: Member dues and local contributions, with little or no central taxation.
views.Business & markets: Guilds and co-ops set standards and trade fairly with each other.
views.Property & land: Tools and workshops owned by members, and land used by the people who work it.
views.Education: Apprenticeship and skill-sharing within the trade and community.
views.Environment & energy: Trade-managed local resources and small-scale sustainable production.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so their guild or co-op takes them in, because the group looks after its own, and mutual aid fills any gaps.
You have a horrible cut, so your guild or co-op's health fund pays for the visit, and you owe nothing more.
You have an idea for a new business, so your guild and a mutual bank back you, so you start within a trade you share with peers.
You lose your job, so your guild or co-op finds you work and supports you from a mutual fund.
You want to buy or build a home, so you build or buy through a guild or co-op housing society.

combos.name: Democratic Socialism
combos.summary: A strong welfare state and public ownership of key industries, kept in check by elections and open markets.

views.Healthcare: Universal, tax-funded, publicly run care.
views.Poverty & welfare: Generous benefits and guarantees, with public housing and strong support.
views.Employment & labor: Strong unions, worker boards and sometimes job guarantees.
views.Taxes: High progressive taxes on income and wealth.
views.Business & markets: Open markets plus public or worker ownership in key sectors and utilities.
views.Property & land: Private property remains, alongside large public and collective stakes in major industries.
views.Education: Free public schools and universities.
views.Environment & energy: Public ownership and heavy investment in clean energy, plus strong standards.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so public housing and a caseworker get them a home quickly, funded by a welfare state.
You have a horrible cut, so a public hospital treats you with tiny fees, because taxes and public ownership pay for it.
You have an idea for a new business, so you start with strong public support, though big sectors are publicly owned and taxes are high.
You lose your job, so generous unemployment pay and a public jobs agency find you a new place.
You want to buy or build a home, so you rent from a large public housing sector or buy with public loans.

combos.name: Libertarian Social Democracy
combos.summary: Nordic-style social programs, delivered in decentralized, voluntary and cooperative ways instead of through large bureaucracies.

views.Healthcare: Universal coverage, but locally run and co-op provided, with patient control.
views.Poverty & welfare: A basic income or dividend from shared resources replaces many separate benefit programs.
views.Employment & labor: Strong unions and co-ops with minimal government job regulation.
views.Taxes: High but simple taxes, focused on land, resources and wealth rather than many levies.
views.Business & markets: Open markets with strong anti-monopoly rules and support for co-ops.
views.Property & land: Private property for goods, with shared ownership of land and natural resources.
views.Education: Public funding with local, parent- and community-run schools.
views.Environment & energy: Resource taxes and dividends make polluters pay, backed by strong standards.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a local voluntary group, funded by the public, finds them housing with less red tape.
You have a horrible cut, so public insurance pays, but you choose a local or cooperative clinic.
You have an idea for a new business, so you start with light rules and public support, with local groups helping you.
You lose your job, so public unemployment pay covers you, and local groups help you retrain.
You want to buy or build a home, so you build with few permits, on shared land, with public loans if needed.

combos.name: Progressive Mixed Economy
combos.summary: Competitive markets with a strong regulatory state, broad social insurance and room for public investment.

views.Healthcare: Regulated insurance with a public option or mandate so everyone is covered.
views.Poverty & welfare: Social insurance plus a safety net and public programs for those in need.
views.Employment & labor: Minimum wage, union rights and worker representation in firms.
views.Taxes: Progressive taxes alongside social insurance contributions.
views.Business & markets: Competitive markets with antitrust and a strong regulatory framework.
views.Property & land: Private property protected, with social obligations and regulation for public benefit.
views.Education: Public schools and subsidized college, with apprenticeship routes.
views.Environment & energy: Regulation and public investment, with market tools like carbon pricing.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so public housing and rent aid get them a place, with the private market offering more options.
You have a horrible cut, so public insurance covers most of it, while private hospitals compete for your visit.
You have an idea for a new business, so you get a bank loan or small-business loan and fair-competition rules protect you from big firms.
You lose your job, so unemployment insurance covers part of your pay while public programs retrain you.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy with a government-backed mortgage in a regulated housing market.

combos.name: Ordoliberalism
combos.summary: A free market with strong rules that guard competition, and a limited but real social safety net.

views.Healthcare: Regulated insurance with competition, and limited public support for those who can't pay.
views.Poverty & welfare: A minimal safety net, with insurance-based support for workers.
views.Employment & labor: Free contracts with basic standards and some worker representation.
views.Taxes: Moderate, simple tax systems with a focus on stability.
views.Business & markets: Strong antitrust and competition rules, with the state keeping the 'rules of the game' fair.
views.Property & land: Strong property rights with limited social obligations.
views.Education: Public schools with choice, plus apprenticeships.
views.Environment & energy: Rules and prices (taxes or trading) set by the state, with markets doing the work.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a limited safety net gives them a bed, and market rules that keep rents fair help them move on.
You have a horrible cut, so your required insurance pays at a competitive, price-checked clinic.
You have an idea for a new business, so you start with light rules and a bank loan, and the state keeps the market fair.
You lose your job, so a small safety net holds you up while the labor market hires you quickly.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy or build with a regulated mortgage and a few permits.

combos.name: Regulated Corporate Capitalism
combos.summary: Large firms dominate the economy, with rules that limit abuse but largely leave them in charge.

views.Healthcare: Large insurers and hospital systems operating under regulation and standards.
views.Poverty & welfare: Limited targeted help tied to work, with growth expected to do most of the lifting.
views.Employment & labor: Large employers set the terms, with minimum standards and legal protections for workers.
views.Taxes: Moderate taxes with breaks and credits for big business.
views.Business & markets: Large firms operate under antitrust, consumer and financial rules, with close ties to regulators.
views.Property & land: Strong corporate and intellectual property rights, with regulation on use.
views.Education: Public and private schools, with strong employer influence on training and research.
views.Environment & energy: Regulations negotiated with industry, plus market incentives and subsidies.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a big developer or charity-run shelter takes them in, with limited public help.
You have a horrible cut, so your job's insurance pays at a big hospital chain, though you may owe a deductible.
You have an idea for a new business, so you seek investors or a bank, with licensing and safety rules to meet, while big firms dominate the market.
You lose your job, so a small unemployment payment helps while you look for work at large firms.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy from a big developer with a bank loan, in a regulated market.

combos.name: Deregulated Capitalism
combos.summary: Free enterprise as the main rule, with only a few basic regulations and low taxes.

views.Healthcare: A mostly private market with light regulation and little public insurance.
views.Poverty & welfare: Charity and a thin safety net with strong work incentives.
views.Employment & labor: Flexible labor markets with few mandates and weak unions.
views.Taxes: Low taxes, especially on investment and business.
views.Business & markets: Competition with only light regulation, and rules removed where possible.
views.Property & land: Strong property rights with limited zoning and environmental restrictions.
views.Education: School choice, vouchers and private options with limited public control.
views.Environment & energy: Fewer rules, with market incentives and courts handling harm.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a private charity gives them a bed, since taxes are low and there are few programs.
You have a horrible cut, so you pay mostly yourself or with private insurance, and there are few limits on the price.
You have an idea for a new business, so you open with minimal rules and low taxes, and you keep most of your profit.
You lose your job, so you rely on savings, and a lightly regulated market hires quickly.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy or build with few permits and a private loan.

combos.name: Guild Socialism
combos.summary: Large public and worker-owned sectors run alongside a strong welfare state, with guilds and unions sharing power over the economy.

views.Healthcare: Universal and publicly run, with unions and local bodies helping manage hospitals and clinics.
views.Poverty & welfare: Generous guaranteed support, with housing and food provided partly through public and cooperative enterprises.
views.Employment & labor: Strong union and guild power, public job guarantees, and workers sitting on the boards of large firms.
views.Taxes: High, progressive taxes on income and wealth fund wide public services and public investment.
views.Business & markets: Key industries are publicly or collectively owned, while smaller firms compete in a regulated market.
views.Property & land: Land and big industry are held in common or by workers, with personal property and homes still private.
views.Education: Free and public through university, with guilds and unions helping run training and apprenticeships.
views.Environment & energy: Public ownership of energy and utilities, with democratic input from workers and communities on climate goals.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so public bodies and guilds house them as a matter of right, and a caseworker finds them a job.
You have a horrible cut, so you are stitched up at a public hospital run by workers and unions, at no cost.
You have an idea for a new business, so you pitch it to a worker-run board or your guild, which funds it and shares the profits, but a private startup is hard.
You lose your job, so unemployment pay and a public jobs agency or your guild place you in new work.
You want to buy or build a home, so you get public or guild housing, with a long wait and little private ownership.

combos.name: Social Democracy
combos.summary: A market economy with a large welfare state, strong unions, and some public ownership of key industries.

views.Healthcare: Universal coverage, paid for publicly, with a mix of public and private providers.
views.Poverty & welfare: Broad safety net with unemployment insurance, pensions, and family support for everyone.
views.Employment & labor: Strong unions and collective bargaining, with a high minimum wage and worker protections.
views.Taxes: High taxes on income, with a mix of consumption and wealth taxes funding public services.
views.Business & markets: Private firms compete, but utilities and key sectors are public or closely regulated.
views.Property & land: Private property is protected, with public ownership of infrastructure and some natural resources.
views.Education: Free public schools and universities, with strong vocational training tied to industry.
views.Environment & energy: Public investment and regulation steer the shift to clean energy, with carbon pricing alongside.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a public housing office and rent aid get them a home, and a caseworker helps them find a job.
You have a horrible cut, so universal insurance covers you at the hospital, and you pay a small fee.
You have an idea for a new business, so you start with public loans and support, inside fair rules, and keep part of the profit after high taxes.
You lose your job, so generous unemployment pay and retraining carry you to the next job.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy with a public loan or rent from a large public housing sector.

combos.name: Welfare Capitalism
combos.summary: Large private firms drive the economy, while government regulation, public insurance, and bargaining soften the risks.

views.Healthcare: Mixed system with private insurers and providers, plus public programs for the poor, old, and disabled.
views.Poverty & welfare: Targeted safety net such as tax credits and unemployment insurance, aimed at those who need it.
views.Employment & labor: Flexible labor markets with minimum wage floors, some union rights, and worker protections.
views.Taxes: Moderate taxes that rise with income, with corporate taxes and deductions used to steer investment.
views.Business & markets: Big firms are welcome but watched, with antitrust, consumer, and financial rules.
views.Property & land: Strong private property, with zoning and regulation shaping how land and assets are used.
views.Education: Public schools plus private options, with student aid helping people reach college.
views.Environment & energy: Regulation, subsidies, and standards push industry toward lower emissions without banning it.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a government safety net gives them a bed, but a private landlord or shelter provides the actual housing.
You have a horrible cut, so private insurance, with public help for the poor, covers the visit, though a big bill is still possible.
You have an idea for a new business, so you raise money from banks or investors, with rules to meet and large firms as competition, so the odds are mixed.
You lose your job, so unemployment insurance pays part of your wage while you look for work.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy with a bank loan or a government-backed mortgage in a regulated market.

combos.name: Cooperative Commonwealth
combos.summary: An economy of worker cooperatives, guilds, and mutual aid, backed by a welfare floor and strong personal freedom.

views.Healthcare: Care provided through mutual aid societies and cooperative clinics, with a public guarantee as backup.
views.Poverty & welfare: Basic needs met through mutual aid, cooperative housing, and a guaranteed income or similar floor.
views.Employment & labor: Workers own and run their firms, with guilds setting standards and cooperatives as the main employer.
views.Taxes: Light-to-moderate taxes, with land and resource taxes used to fund a basic dividend and shared services.
views.Business & markets: Markets of cooperatives and small producers, with credit supplied by mutual banks and no big shareholders.
views.Property & land: Workplaces are owned by the workers, and land is held by communities, with rent shared by all.
views.Education: Public and community-run learning, with guild apprenticeships and cooperative schools.
views.Environment & energy: Local control with shared limits on pollution, and communities able to protect their own land and water.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a co-op or guild takes them in, and a basic income keeps them going until they find work.
You have a horrible cut, so a cooperative or guild clinic treats you, with a public floor of coverage behind it.
You have an idea for a new business, so you form a co-op or join a guild, and a basic income cushions the risk.
You lose your job, so your guild or co-op and a public floor carry you until you find work.
You want to buy or build a home, so you build or buy through a co-op, on community land, with public loans if needed.

combos.name: Inclusive Market Economy
combos.summary: Open, competitive markets with a basic safety net and strong rights, but little central planning.

views.Healthcare: Universal basic coverage, often through regulated insurance or vouchers, with competition among providers.
views.Poverty & welfare: A simple, wide floor such as a basic income or negative income tax, in place of many separate programs.
views.Employment & labor: Open labor markets with basic worker protections and freedom to organize, but few mandated rules.
views.Taxes: A simple, broad tax system with few loopholes, plus taxes on land or pollution.
views.Business & markets: Competition is encouraged and monopolies are broken up, with rules mostly aimed at keeping markets fair.
views.Property & land: Strong private property, with land and natural resource rents shared with the public.
views.Education: Publicly funded but with school choice, so families and students can pick providers.
views.Environment & energy: Market tools like carbon taxes and tradable permits are used to cut pollution at low cost.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a basic income and open building rules let them rent a place of their own.
You have a horrible cut, so you choose any clinic, and universal basic coverage pays for most of it.
You have an idea for a new business, so you start with few barriers and a bank loan, and a basic income softens a failure.
You lose your job, so a basic income and a flexible market get you back to work quickly.
You want to buy or build a home, so you build or buy easily with a simple mortgage, with land rent shared by all.

combos.name: Free Enterprise Economy
combos.summary: Private business and open competition lead the economy, with limited government rules and a small safety net.

views.Healthcare: Mostly private care and insurance, with limited public help for those who cannot afford it.
views.Poverty & welfare: A small safety net, with most help coming from families, charities, and work requirements.
views.Employment & labor: Flexible hiring and firing, few union mandates, and wages set mostly by supply and demand.
views.Taxes: Low, broad taxes with lower rates on business and investment to encourage growth.
views.Business & markets: Open competition with light regulation, rules mostly limited to fraud, contracts, and basic safety.
views.Property & land: Strong private property rights over land, business, and assets, with little government control.
views.Education: Mix of private and charter schools, with parents free to choose and pay for what they want.
views.Environment & energy: Prefers market solutions and private property rights over mandates, with limited government rules on energy.

examples: A homeless person is in need of aid, so a charity and a small safety net are what they have, since the market is expected to do the rest.
You have a horrible cut, so you are treated at a private hospital, paying with insurance or out of pocket.
You have an idea for a new business, so you open with light rules, low taxes, and private funding, and you keep most of what you earn.
You lose your job, so you live on savings while a lightly regulated market hires quickly.
You want to buy or build a home, so you buy or build with few permits and a private loan, and the market sets the price.
